posts.name: Arcanist Lupus
posts.cooked:
Powers, Plays, and Draws are all necessary for a successful hero.  But for each hero the limiting factors are different.

Wraith and AA, for example are frequently limited by the number of power uses (for all that they get extra).  I see them both often with oodles of cards in their hands and nothing worth playing.

Mr. Fixer, on the other hand, can benefit from one extra power each turn, and that's it.  All others are useless.  Unity often doesn't even have a use for one free power.

Nightmist and Scholar live by their hand sizes.  Extra cards never go to waste.  

Tachyon burns through her hand far faster than she knows what to do with, and would much rather have extra draws than plays.

Parse has enough card draw to keep her happy for a century - unless she plays Snap Decision, in which case she starts burning through her hand like a house on fire.  And she frequently has more powers than she knows what to do with.

I could go on and on.

posts.name: Foote
posts.cooked:
So is your vote, "action diversity is better except for solely Team Leader Tachyon's specific brand of action amplification?

No, I don't think I'd say that. I think they are all pretty equal, at least in terms of how you win games easier. I think card draw is an outlier worthy of discussion though, which has certainly sparked some good thoughts.

Pure Card Draw is great until you've saturated your hand with all your options

Totally. This goes back to a point that Pydro made as well where he feels that card draw looses value when your hand is already flush with options. It's a valid point for sure. But I think we have different views on what the value of card draw actually is. From a strictly pragmatic lens, it's difficult to disagree with both of you on this point. My question for both of you is do you think that Card Draw should only be viewed from a strict pragmatic stance? In regards to play and power actions, my opinion is a resounding yes. But for Card Draw I question that. Whether you have the answers in your hand or not for the current play action is almost irrelevent to me when looking at the value of digging through your deck faster to get to the next answer, and the one after that. The value of card draw from this lens never diminishes (unless you have near your entire deck in your hand at once, then you probably hit some diminishing returns on that value, but I've never seen that outside of crazy Nightmist shenanigans) 

I come from a competitive card game background like many of you (Magic, Hearthstone, ect.). Does my previous competitive gaming experience force me to give too much value into card advantage in a game such as SotM? This is more self reflective for sure, but maybe that helps others to see where I'm coming from if they are familiar with deck based game theory such Tempo and Card Advantage (more on tempo later). It's quite possible I do, but at this point I do not believe so.
 

I always find card draw a weak action. It's great when your hand size is low, of course, but it's just, if there's nothing better to do, draw a card.

When you are getting into situations where you have "nothing better to do", then you likely did not gauge the value of card draw appropriatly prior to that situation. One thing I should probably note here that I overlooked previously is that drawing cards isn't preventing you from doing the other actions. I want to make it clear that I am not in anyway talking about the edge rule of skipping your play and power phase to take the draw phase twice. While the value of card draw in my mind holds consistent high value, I don't agree that it's always going to be higher than the value of the lost tempo by skipping your other two important phases. This of course is also subjective, since this tempo loss is not as big of a deal with certain decks (ex. Expatriete). 

You are not alone in your feelings of card draw. A lot of people think it's a waste, especially if it's comming at the cost of tempo or other flashy abilities and combos. It doesn't always "feel" great. But I'd like to ask you to reevaluate your opinion here as it truely is an understated yet powerful action. 

I find card draw's strength scales with how much you do it. Doing it once is not that strong, but doing it many times is extremely strong

This is correct in my view. I think I breifly skimmed this before, but Card Draw's value does indeed increase exponentially.

posts.name: Jeysie
posts.cooked:
The difference with Magic is stuff like how you can play as many cards in a turn as you want so long as you can pay for it, how usually you only get to use a card once, and how you usually only get to go through your deck once. It's a lot easier to trade cards 1-1 in terms of removal and counters. Your opponent is often building up to their deck's payoff turn by turn. So card draw is more important because you really need to make sure to have the right card at precisely the right time. Also you can only have seven cards before needing to discard.

Sentinels has a lot of stuff that changes that dynamic significantly. You typically only get to play one card per turn. You can cycle through your deck as many times as you need to. Even before that pulling stuff back out of your trash is often much easier and less costly. The number of cards that can trade 1-1 for a threat are more limited in number. The villain board state tends to vary more from turn to turn rather than slowly building up to a finale you're racing against.

So I feel it's a lot easier to end up with a clogged hand in Sentinels than it is with Magic. Sure, it can be useful being in situations where you can basically play any card in your deck any time you need it, but a lot of the time cards in Sentinels are way better when they're actually on the board than when they're in potentia.

posts.name: corran109
posts.cooked:
That's true, Sentinels is more dynamic. There's a balance to be struck though. Early on in a Sentinel game, I'd pick drawing cards over dealing with a very minor threat. Cards are better on the board, but they have to be available for that. To me, card draw means trading taking a direct action now to make a more potent direct action later. There are some cases where that trade off won't be worth it, but for my playstyle there are plenty of cases where that trade off is very worth it.

Even later in the game when things are more bleak, there are times when your direct actions will help only a small amount, but you know there are cards in your deck that can be more helpful in the coming turns, at which point the more you get through your deck the better.

posts.name: Jeysie

Yeah, The Sentinels getting their entire deck in their hand is not too difficult. Haka and sometimes Scholar and Naturalist are good for that too.

I think that in terms of card draw versus play, there's different categories of characters regards who wants cards on the table, who wants specific cards on the table, who wants a big hand, who wants to play all the things, etc.

Some characters like AZ, Bunker, Expat, are hard to use at all unless they have very specific cards on the table.

Some folks like Fixer and Wraith tend to operate where you want specific cards on the table but then they almost never need to play much else afterwards.

Folks like Legacy, Argent, Omnitron-X, Unity, often want all their things on the table as soon as you can get it there, since their per-turn options are more dependent on their board than on their hand.

Folks like Scholar and Nightmist usually want huge hands for discard fodder all the time.

Folks like Tachyon and Fanatic want to be tossing one-shots around a lot.

Finally you get folks like Parse & Vis whose playstyles are highly dependant on the overall board state.

So there's basically some folks who can never have enough card draw, some who want to initially filter through their deck but then care more about card play or extra power use afterwards, and some who can never have enough card play.

posts.name: phantaskippy
posts.cooked:
I missed a bunch of discussion.

  Here's my thoughts.

Disclaimer:  of course exceptions don't just exist, but abound in sentinels, we all know them, so i'm not covering them.

1.  Card Play:  card play is strongest when your play area is empty, and for most heroes, diminishes as you get more cards in play.  Extra card play early is incredibly valuable, letting you set up faster, get in front of limited destruction, and generally get past the initial set up of most villains faster and in better shape.  In my experience, the better you handle the initial villain set up and the faster you recover from destruction/reach  the more likely you are to win, that is why in my value system, card play is the most powerful of the 3 actions.

2.  Powers:  powers always have value, because heroes have innate powers, but they tend to increase in value as heroes get more cards in play.  They tend to be less valuable early, because innate powers tend to be less powerful than one shots, and rarely accelerate setup.  Powers are stronger the more setup heroes have, and also when card play options diminish due to hand size.

3.  Card Draw:  card draw is most valuable when your hand is empty, and loses value as you get better cards in your hand.  Card draw increases your options, but once you have the best option in hand adding more cards will not help your next card play, but only increase probability that you'll have the best card later.  Card draw value reaches 0 once you have access to all your options.

Card draw is also more complex, because it does nothing immediately, it has probability of improving later actions, but no direct impact.  Team Leader is the best example of this.  The card draw is fantastic, it makes the team almost completely immune to hand denial, and gives everyone more options constantly.  Once you have 10 or more cards in hand though, it isn't likely to improve your next card play so much that you would take more cards over using a power or playing a card.  At that point (H) card draws aren't even worth a power use, let alone a card play.  That's one reason Team Leader gets replaced by Research Grant eventually, because that discard becomes more valuable than every other hero getting a card (unless they can discard for damage on their own).

The value for each is dynamic, if your area is empty card play is best, if your hand is empty, card draw, if you are setup powers.

My work on valuing the health impact of each (from right after Shattered Timelines) ended with card play at roughly 3 points, powers at roughly 2 points, and card draw at roughly 1 point.

That means Team Leader is valued at (H) points, making it one of the stronger powers in the game.  (Of course it isn't perfect, card draw is actually stronger in low (H) games, because increasing options for hero play from 12 to 13 is more valuable than increasing from 20 to 21, or to put it another way, the more hands and card plays your team has, the more likely one of you has a card to deal with the current situation, so digging for the right card drops in value)

But again, that valuation is from my own testing, which means it is biased by the data coming solely from games and experiments I was running.  Im my experience early game strength and recovery from destruction are the most important factors in a win or loss, averaged across all villains.

Also, note that while I finished the process and came upbwith the 3-2-1 point valuation, the real answer is "it depends", because each situation in Sentinels is so unique.  The chief value of the process has been the ability to look at innate powers in playtesting with a rough guide on how good they are.

A fun thing from that process:  Impromptu Invention gives you a card draw (1), a card play (3), a search that hits the majority of valuable cards in your deck (this effect came out to around 5 points of value) and playing that card (3), for a total value of 12 points, which beats every other card in the game that isn't Wrathful Retribution (which came out around 17, and was a hard one to value), which was good, because I would have considered the process invalid if it hadn't.

posts.name: corran109
posts.cooked:
My problem with that system is that it assumes every card play and every power has the same level of effect. Even if everyone has 10 cards in hand, there are occasions where you want to draw more cards. Say you're at MMFFCC and you want to your team to draw another environment affecting card.

Play and Power's effects are always visible, where Draw's power is in its potential. Is there something you want from your deck that really helps against the boss or an upcoming situation? There's a lot of potential power in that siuation. Draw also directly informs Play's power. While Mr. Fixer can get to a situation where he has all he needs on his board, he can also get to a situation where he has a dead hand, with only tools and styles in it. While using a power would be more directly powerful in that situation, more card draw to get him to his one-shots is arguably more useful in that situation (unless there's something that needs to die right now).

Ultimately though, since this is a cooperative game, it's easy to discuss at the table what the best option is, and it'll always depend on the board states of 3-5 heros, an environment, and the villian(s).

P.S. Taking a moment to go back to Magic, there's a idiom in Magic that is somewhat relevant to this discussion: The only point of life that matters is your last. That is to say, HP is a resource just like everything else. While this is intrinsic to the game, it's not always concious. For Magic itself, early on, the devs didn't value card draw and really valued life gain. This is apparent in the cost of both effects and expansions came out. Card draw got more expensive and life gain got less expensive. While Sentinels is very different since life gain can be very important with the way damage comes out, there's still a point to be had here. I'll usually value drawing a card over preventing a couple points of damage. If I'm not set up yet, I'll use Bunker's draw over using his Flak Cannon to kill something that might only do 2 damage, for a more specific example.

posts.name: phantaskippy
posts.cooked:
The potential isn't that hard to quantify, since every card draw does 2 things, first it moves each card in your deck one draw closer to your hand, and 2, it increases the odds that a given card is in your hand already.  That's why card draw stacking has such value.

It isn't that card draw isn't valuable, it is.  It is just not affecting the fight directly.  Like we have both stated, card draw's value is chiefly the probability that the top card of your deck would be more helpful than the ones in your hand.

Situationally, like when there is an ongoing/env. card that needs to go away before you go after the villain and you don't have a destruction card in hand, that card draw holds the possibility of providing great value.  But it still only holds a percentage chance of providing that value, and even then the value can often seem more than it actually is.

Lwets run some numbers.  Let's say you have drawn 6 cards since the start of the game, and no  RPG Launcher, and now Baron Blade has Backlash field in play.  The chance that Argent Adept giving you a draw will get you RPG launcher is 10%.  RPG Launcher being played 1 round early has a value of 12 in a 4 player game.  A 10% chance of getting a 12 point play is still only worth 1.2 points.  Now if your deck is full of cards that are better than what is in your hand then the point values will be different because the odds of providing at least some value are much better than just 10%.  But if you have shotgun in play and cryo rounds in hand, that card draw isn't a better value better than just pushing through the damage.

posts.name: corran109
posts.cooked:
But it's not just the RPG launcher's vaule you'd have to calculate, but the value of every card that's drawn a turn before you would have drawn them. If the turn after you draw the RPG launcher you draw Hollow Points which let you ensure a crucial minion kill the round after, that also increases the value of the single card draw. Assuming you've drawn 6 cards, a single card draw affects up to 34 cards, depending on the length of the game, and there's a lot of potential there.

Then there'sthe question is also how much of an impact the shotgun or the cryo rounds will be at this point in time. At this point in depends on your playstyle. For me, I'd rather take a couple points of damage to ensure higher potential later via draw. But also that using the shotgun might not net you anything besides 4 damage on the boss and using cryo rounds might end up futile if you use it to kill a 4 health minion the next turn. I primarily don't agree with "card play = 3 points and power = 2" unless you're talking averages, but then that still undervalues card draw in my opinion.

posts.name: Pydro
posts.cooked:
I think it is even more complicated than that for a couple of reasons:

Some very powerful cards have to come at the right time. For example, drawing cards to get Turret Mode while you have both guns would be helpful. However, since it will take you two turns to play those cards then Turret Mode. If Turret Mode is one of the two cards on top and you would have drawn it anyways, the value of the card draw driops. Just the first example I thought of, but most of the time you don't know that and would want to draw anyways. However, my personnal play style is that if I have a few cards I want to play, I don't worry about card draw since I know I will naturally draw a few cards before I need to play something else.

Another huge issue is game length. If you wouldn't have drawn a card because of the game would have ended, and now due to card draw you would have drawn that card, that greatly increases the value.

Related to this is that the value of the cards drastically change based on when the game would potentially end. Defensive cards, or limiting damage, can be great if they matter. If you can pump out enough damage so that even if you take everything you still win, the value of those cards go down. This is something that constantly changes throughout the game, and can effect drawing for certain cards. I think trying to find out what cards are really important based on what is needed is one of the most important skills of SotM.

It also matters what other options you have. Visionary allowing someone to draw cards is big, even if the draw value is low, because she doesn't always have other powers that are worth it.

Related to this is that when I look at card draw, I don't look at what is the next card, I think," what if I do this same action 5 times, and only then get the card I need." Now, I have to find the value of all those cards against using up my resources for repeating the same action over and over. If that action could have been damage, that could have been a lot of damage that was now lost, and potentially finish the game. Was all of those actions worth it digging for that one card. Well, it depends on the situation, what the card is, and what I am giving up.

posts.name: Dandolo
posts.cooked:
Really interesting discussion. I’ve also put some thought as to into how powerful these effects are “on average” since it varies so much based on situation.

The values I came up with were:
1 pt: 1 damage
2 pts: 1 card draw
3 pts: 1 card play or 1 power use or 4 HP recovered

The way I arrived at these numbers was by playing a bunch of games and trying to pay attention to cases where there’s a choice between 2 effects and which effect I’m choosing most frequently. For example, I find that when using Proverbs and Axioms I’ll take the HP recovery over the power more often then not, which suggests to me that 5 Hero HP is generally worth more to me than 1 power use. Or if I have a choice of any of AA’s rhythm accompanys I’ll pick “play” the most frequently and 1 damage the least frequently.

Having values like these in your back pocket is most useful for things like playtesting or attempting to balance custom content… but when just playing a game, it’s almost always better to focus on the board state at that exact moment rather than loose numerical values like these.

As to the original question of action diversity versus action amplification… I would say it’s not really a question of which is more useful as much as how much amplification does it take to make up for a loss of action diversity. As a starting point, I’d suggest setting up a couple of games with Benchmark and Normal Skyscraper incapacitated and 3 other heroes. Treat the games as H=4 and see if they’re easier or harder than a generic 4 hero game.

posts.name: phantaskippy
posts.cooked:
Drawing cards instead of an action that progresses the game toward a victorious ending lengthens the game.  Which has negative value that needs to be factored in.

I understand the desire to see your hero get to their most powerful version, but stretching the game to reach that point almost always increases your chance of losing.  There are places for card draw to take precedent, but they are more rare than common.

I know my main post was long, but a lot of the points you are making are in it.  It is an average, it isn't universal, because situationality is a key factor in SotM, and a lot of the pro points were investigated.

One problem with the "every card is moved up 1" is that those cards aren't entering play, just your hand.  And the value added by each card getting moved up one is offset largely by whether those cards are better than options you already have.

That's why the idea that card draw stacking is really powerful is largely false, because you almost always reduce the value of future draws once your hand gets big, unless you can internally discard for value (which is value added to discards by other cards, not value inherent to card draw).

Getting a hand full of great cards is awesome, but in the time you spend playing those cards the value of every card you continue to draw has been reduced, because you have reduced the odds that that card will be better than what is in your hand.

Card draw stacking does add value to the team, but the more you do it, the less value each individual card draw has.
